findings.title: Routine cleanup progress logged at Error level
findings.body:
In the new CleanAnnotations/CleanOrphanedAnnotationTags code, routine informational messages are logged with r.log.Error even on success. For example:
```
r.log.Error("Annotations to clean by time", "count", len(ids), "ids", ids, "cond", cond, "err", err)
...
r.log.Error("cleaned annotations by time", "count", len(ids), "affected", x, "err", y)
```
These messages are emitted on the happy path (the call to fetchIDs has already returned a non-nil error short-circuit before the first Error log is reached, and deleteByIDs returns success in the second). Error-level logging is reserved for actual failures, and using it for normal per-batch progress will spam production logs, trip log-based alerting, and obscure real errors. These should be r.log.Info or r.log.Debug.

findings.title: Nil error logged as err field on success
findings.body: Multiple new log calls include `"err", err` after the error has already been checked and returned (e.g. lines 534, 537, 554, 557, 576, 579). On the happy path err is nil, so the resulting structured log entry looks like `"err": null` for a successful batch. This is misleading to operators who scan logs for `"err":` fields and makes it look like every cleanup batch is failing. The err key should only be included when an error is actually present.

findings.title: Undocumented 10x ticker frequency change affects all cleanup jobs
findings.body:
The cleanup ticker is changed from 10 minutes to 1 minute:
```
- ticker := time.NewTicker(time.Minute * 10)
+ ticker := time.NewTicker(time.Minute * 1)
```
This is not mentioned in the PR description and is unrelated to the MySQL deadlock fix. It increases the run frequency of *every* job in clean() (tmp files, expired snapshots, dashboard versions, expired images, annotations, user invites, short URLs, query history) by 10x, multiplying DB load and the chance of overlapping long-running cleanups against the 9-minute per-cycle timeout. If the change is intentional (e.g. to compensate for accumulation during the deadlock period), it needs its own justification, and the PR description and release notes must call it out so operators can adjust. Ideally the cleanup interval should be configurable rather than hard-coded.

findings.title: O(n^2) string building in SQLite large-batch path
findings.body:
The SQLite parameter-limit workaround builds the IN-list with repeated fmt.Sprintf:
```
values := fmt.Sprint(ids[0])
for _, v := range ids[1:] {
    values = fmt.Sprintf("%s, %d", values, v)
}
```
This is O(n^2) in both time and allocations because each step copies the entire growing string. With the batch size used in the new test (32767) this is tens of millions of bytes copied. The same job can be done in O(n) with a strings.Builder and strconv.AppendInt. The path is also only triggered when batch size exceeds the SQLite parameter limit, so it is exercised by the new integration test and the cost matters.

findings.title: fetchIDs concatenates table name and condition into SQL
findings.body:
fetchIDs builds SQL via fmt.Sprintf with the table name and the WHERE clause as opaque strings:
```
sql := fmt.Sprintf(`SELECT id FROM %s`, table)
sql += fmt.Sprintf(` WHERE %s`, condition)
```
Today every call site passes a constant string so there is no immediate injection, but the signature invites future callers to pass user-controlled fragments. Either make the table an enumerated constant or compose the predicate through bound parameters, so the function cannot be misused.
